name: Amira Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I walk the old market district, the covered market, the bus station and the streets behind it. Foot patrol, eight-hour shifts, mostly days. I know half the stallholders by name, and they tell me who's been shoplifting before I ask. I like that people wave. What wears me out is the paperwork after every arrest, and the new tablet they gave us, which I mostly avoid.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a studio above a bakery on Station Lane, on my own. I send my mum about a hundred and fifty a month, because her cleaning hours got cut last spring. After that, there's not much left; I have maybe three weeks of money saved. And the city force is the only police job around here, so I don't have many options if this goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave us alone and let us do the job. I don't need a computer to tell me which stallholder is having a bad week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI isn't what keeps me up. The force wants to merge the market station into the central one, and then my foot beat probably goes. It's all about saving money. Add my mum's hours, and I'm stretched whatever the computers do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and doing the beat properly so nobody can say it's not needed. I'd stop buying lunch from the stalls, which is about forty a week, and bring food from home. And I'd keep sending Mum her money, because that's not up for discussion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired and a bit stuck. Nothing's getting worse because of AI, but nothing's getting better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you if the market station merges?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably be put on response cars out of central, rotating shifts, nights included. Same pay, more or less, but I'd lose the people I know. And night shifts make it hard to get over to Mum's on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you avoid the tablet. Does that cause trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sergeant reminds me, and I fill it in at the end of the week instead of every day. I'm not good with it, and I don't trust things I can't see inside. Paper you can read twice.

say: Leave us **alone** to do the job; a computer can't read the stallholders.
The **foot beat** works because people know us by name.
think: The real threat is the **station merger**, which could end my foot beat.
With my **mum's hours cut**, I'm stretched whatever happens with AI.
do: Keep doing the **market beat** properly so nobody can call it unnecessary.
Bring **lunch from home** to save about forty a week.
Keep sending **150 a month** to my mum.
feel: **Tired and stuck**, with nothing getting better on its own.
S0.quote: AI isn't what keeps me up. The force wants to merge the market station into the central one, and then my foot beat probably goes.
fieldNote: Amira's pressures are **budget and family**, not technology.
She avoids the tablet and **trusts paper**, which may count against her later.
Supporting her **mother** is fixed; everything else bends around it.

steps.text: Keep walking the market beat on every shift
Bring lunch from home to save about forty a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say be careful. The people in the market don't want a chatbot; they want to see an officer. I'd say that to the sergeant and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the station merger gets pushed through faster, because they'd say AI does the admin and fewer officers can cover more ground. I'm average and slow with the tablet, so if they're picking who stays on the beat, I'm not first in line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mostly wait and see what the force actually brings in, because they announce things that never happen. If they made training compulsory, I'd go, but I wouldn't volunteer. I'd keep the lunch savings going and try to put aside an extra twenty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, in a low, constant way. Like a dripping tap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would make you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A letter. If the force writes to say my post is under review, I'd move then. Until then, I'm not spending money I don't have on courses that might be pointless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the market?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Dogan (an old spice seller in the market) calls me when kids cause trouble, and he'll never use a phone app instead. People like him just stop reporting things.

say: Market traders want to **see an officer**, not use a chatbot.
I'd tell the **sergeant** to be careful with new systems and leave it there.
think: AI admin gives the force a reason to **push the merger** through faster.
Being **slow with the tablet**, I wouldn't be first in line to stay on the beat.
do: **Wait and see** what the force actually brings in before acting.
Save an **extra twenty a week** on top of the lunch savings.
feel: **Worried** in a low, constant way, like a dripping tap.
S1.quote: Mr Dogan (an old spice seller in the market) calls me when kids cause trouble, and he'll never use a phone app instead.
fieldNote: She waits for a **formal letter** before acting; risk-averse and practical.
Worries about **community trust** if reporting goes through apps.
Honest that her **tablet skills** put her at a disadvantage.

steps.text: Wait for a written notice before spending on any course
Save an extra twenty a week on top of lunch savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody should slow it down. I'm not political, but that's common sense: two years isn't enough for anyone to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be finished as a police officer within a few years. By 2028 all the reports, the case files, the call handling are done by AI, and the force will need fewer of us. When the robots come in 2031, foot patrol is an easy one to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give up the studio and move back in with Mum in her flat in Westfield, which saves us both money. I'd cut everything else to the bone. Then I'd look for anything hands-on that lasts longer, like hospital security or the prison service, because those still need people for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared. I don't have a plan B, and I'm not the type to make one fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving back in with your mum: how would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Moving back in with my mum at twenty-seven would be embarrassing, but it's what families do. Mum would be glad, honestly, and it'd stop me sending money I can't spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do the three years before the robots help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They give me time to get out before the beat goes. But everyone in the force would be doing the same thing, chasing the same few security jobs. I'd be competing with people who are better with computers than me.

say: Two years is **too fast**, and somebody should slow it down.
It's **common sense**, not politics, that nobody can adjust that quickly.
think: I'd be **finished as an officer** within a few years of 2028.
When robots come in 2031, **foot patrol** is an easy one to replace.
do: Give up the studio and **move in with Mum** in Westfield.
Apply for **hospital security** or prison service jobs that need people longer.
feel: **Properly scared**, with no plan B and no habit of making one fast.
S2.quote: Moving back in with my mum at twenty-seven would be embarrassing, but it's what families do.
fieldNote: Amira expects to **lose her job**, and her answer is family, not retraining.
She thinks the **three-year robot gap** just means a crowded race for security jobs.
**Resistance to change** leaves her with few moves beyond cutting back.

steps.text: Give up the studio and move into Mum's flat in Westfield
Cut spending to rent share, food and travel
Apply for hospital security or prison service jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, slow it down, but at least five years gives people a chance. I'd say it to the sergeant and to my mum, that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd still have the beat until about 2031, then less, then by 2034 probably nothing. I'd be thirty-two when the paperwork goes and thirty-five with no job. That's young enough to start again, but I don't know what as.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get one month saved and then two, by keeping the lunch habit and skipping holidays. Around year three, I'd start applying for jobs that are hands-on and need a person, maybe the prison service. I wouldn't do a course unless the force paid and told me which one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened, but slower. Five years feels like knowing the eviction letter is coming next year, not next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the prison service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Yusuf (a prison officer) says they're always short of staff and it's still about people. I don't love the idea of being inside walls all day. But it's a uniform and a pension, and I know how to handle a difficult person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if this goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody in particular. The companies, maybe, for rushing. The government for not keeping up. I don't think shouting changes much, so I'd rather just get ready.

say: Slow it down, but **five years** at least gives people a chance.
I'd mostly say it to the **sergeant and my mum**, not online.
think: I'd be **thirty-five with no job** by 2034 if the beat goes.
I'm young enough to start again but **don't know as what**.
do: Save up to **two months** by keeping the lunch habit and skipping holidays.
Apply to the **prison service** around year three.
Only take a course if the **force pays** and chooses it.
feel: **Frightened** but slower, like an eviction letter due next year, not next week.
S3.quote: Five years feels like knowing the eviction letter is coming next year, not next week.
fieldNote: She blames **nobody strongly**, true to her centrist, practical outlook.
The **prison service** idea comes from family, not research.
Extra time eases the pace of fear but **not the outcome** she expects.

steps.text: Build savings to two months by skipping holidays
Apply to the prison service around 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair warning, so there's no excuse for anyone not to be ready. Including me, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd stay on the beat for most of the decade, and I'd like that. By 2036 the admin goes, by 2039 the patrol. I'd be thirty-seven, and that scares me less than thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job, and I'd wait a few years to see what actually happens before changing anything. Meanwhile I'd save a bit more every year and try to get my mum on a better footing so she doesn't need my money. If the force offered a transfer to a hands-on role, I'd take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Uneasy, but I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd wait. Isn't ten years a reason to start early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, for someone who likes change. I don't. I'd rather wait until I know what's real and then move once, properly, than chase every rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help your mum get on a better footing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If she got her hours back or a pension top-up, I'd stop sending money and save it instead. That one thing would change my whole year.

say: Ten years is **fair warning**, so nobody has an excuse not to be ready.
think: I'd stay on the **beat** for most of the decade, which I'd like.
Being **thirty-seven** when robots come scares me less than thirty-two.
do: **Wait a few years** to see what's real before changing anything.
Save a bit **more each year** and help Mum need less money.
Take a **hands-on transfer** if the force offers one.
feel: **Calmer** and uneasy, but able to breathe.
S4.quote: I'd rather wait until I know what's real and then move once, properly, than chase every rumour.
fieldNote: Even with a decade, Amira prefers to **move once**, late and carefully.
Her mother's finances are the **lever** that would most change her year.
Still anxious because her **income depends** on a beat she expects to vanish.

steps.text: Wait a few years before making any career move
Raise monthly savings each year as Mum's needs drop
Ask for a hands-on transfer if the force offers one

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. No time, no money, and I'm not quick with new things. What would help is the force telling us early and honestly which jobs are going, and helping officers like me move into other public jobs that still need people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my mum. Half my decisions are about my mum, so any help for me is help for her too. If the government thinks about families like ours, that matters more than any course.

headlineQuote: Half my decisions are about my mum, so any help for me is help for her too.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old foot patrol officer** in the old market district who lives alone in a studio.
She sends her mother **150 a month** and has about three weeks of savings.
She avoids the **tablet and AI tools** and prefers paper she can read twice.
She expects fast AGI to **end her police job** and would move back in with her mother.
Given more time, she'd still **wait and move once**, probably into a hands-on public job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time, no money and no quick way for her to adapt.
whatWouldHelp: **Early, honest notice** of which jobs are going, plus help moving into other public jobs.
